page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: The target
lines: The cell envelope of the bacterium is the
part targeted, and within the envelope it is
the cell wall that holds the stain.
The envelope has three layers: glycocalyx,
steps.why: Gram staining works only because bacteria differ in their envelope, so the envelope — and the peptidoglycan wall inside it — is what the stain is testing. The book answers 'cell envelope' alone; naming the wall inside it is what makes the answer complete.
common_mistakes: Answering the nucleoid or the ribosome. The stain never reports on them.
Writing plasma membrane alone. It is the wall inside the envelope that holds the stain.
steps.memory_tip: Three envelope layers, outside in: glycocalyx, cell wall, plasma membrane.
steps.margin_note: Say cell envelope, then name the cell wall inside it.

steps.label: The two groups
lines: Bacteria whose wall has a thick peptidoglycan
layer keep the crystal violet stain and look
Bacteria with a thin layer lose that stain and
take the counterstain — these are Gram
steps.why: Both results of the test come from one difference: how thick the peptidoglycan layer is. That is the reason the wall is the target.
common_mistakes: Writing that Gram negative bacteria have no cell wall. They have a thin one.
Writing that the stain enters the nucleoid.
steps.memory_tip: Positive keeps the purple; negative loses it.
steps.margin_note: Naming Gram positive and Gram negative earns this mark.

insider_note: The book answers this in five words. Naming the peptidoglycan wall and the two groups is what turns it into a full 2-mark answer.
